title: India, US Ironing Out Trade Deal Differences, Nearing a 'Landing Point': Jaishankar
excerpt: External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar told the Bloomberg New Economy Forum that negotiators are working through the last differences on the bilateral trade pact, even as he stressed that the strategic partnership itself is unchanged.
body:
• External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said India-US trade negotiations are heading towards a "landing point," with trade ministers and the USTR ironing out remaining differences.
  • His comments came just over a week after Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman described the talks as having reached a "plateau."
  • India is seeking better tariff terms than competing economies get in the US market; US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said a deal is being finalised but is not imminent.
  • For Indian exporters and diaspora businesses, the outcome decides whether last year's punitive US tariffs on Indian goods are rolled back.

India and the United States are continuing to engage to iron out differences on their proposed trade deal, and the negotiations are heading towards a "landing point," External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum on Tuesday evening, according to The Hindu. He added that the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remain unchanged.

Asked about the status of the talks, Jaishankar declined to disclose details. He said India's commerce and industry minister, the US Trade Representative and other officials are engaged in working the pact forward.

"My sense is that this is an issue which is heading towards a landing point."

— S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister

Competitor tariffs are the sticking point

Jaishankar framed the remaining work as two-sided: what India and the US settle between themselves, and how India fares against competing economies that are negotiating their own arrangements with Washington. That second part, he noted, is not entirely clear because not every economy has worked out a deal. India is seeking better tariffs than its competitors for its goods in the US market.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=9BAFBjzoImc

The two sides have been in talks since early 2025 on a pact meant to address tariff friction, eliminate non-tariff barriers and boost bilateral market access. Earlier this month, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the two countries were working to finalise a bilateral trade deal but that an agreement was not imminent, and that they had identified the issues that remained unresolved.

A relationship under strain

The negotiations follow a sharp downturn in ties after Washington imposed punitive tariffs on India last year, and after President Donald Trump's assertions about his role in de-escalating the May 2025 India-Pakistan military clashes drew a sharp reaction from Indian officials. Washington's new immigration policy and its H-1B visa fee increase added to the slide, and ties came under fresh strain after the US restricted a key green-card processing programme for major global and Indian IT firms, including Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro — a move we covered in our reporting on the latest US immigration rule changes.

Jaishankar also addressed Washington's broader economic turn, arguing that the US is determined to re-industrialise and to reset the terms of access to its economy, and that the tariff debate is a symptom of that shift. Every significant economy, he said, is now negotiating with the United States on those terms — and India, in his assessment, is "pretty far advanced" in that process.

Partnership, not alliance

On the strategic relationship, Jaishankar drew a line India has held for two decades: the two countries have built convergences and shared interests, but India is not a treaty ally, and that framework has not fundamentally changed. The US, he noted, is revising the terms of its alliances and treaty relationships, with the sentiment felt most strongly in Europe and parts of East Asia.

What to watch

No date was given for a signing. The next signals will be whether Greer's office moves from "not imminent" to a scheduled announcement, and whether the final terms give Indian goods a tariff edge over competitor economies — the test Jaishankar himself set for the deal.
